name: Body language / presence training

lead: Training an open stance, steady eye contact and slower movement is meant to make you come across as more confident and commanding.

Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space. Power-posing research found a reliable effect on how people feel but not on hormones, and an unclear effect on behaviour. Gesture meanings also vary across cultures.

paras: People rehearse in front of a mirror or on video, work on pace, posture and eye contact in conversation, and combine it with grooming and posture work. Practice builds over weeks.
Low risk. Gestures and eye contact can be read differently across cultures.

chain: Open stance, eye contact, slower pace
angle.text: Open stance, steady eye contact and slower movement are practised to make you appear more confident and commanding, often alongside posture and grooming. Research supports increased felt confidence more than measured changes in how others judge the person.

lead: Body language or presence training is the deliberate practice of nonverbal behaviour, such as an open stance, steady eye contact, slower movements and an upright carriage, so as to come across as more confident, warm and commanding. In appearance communities it is treated as the part of looks that moves: two people with the same face can leave different impressions depending on how they hold and present themselves.[1][2]

Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space, mostly occurring without conscious awareness, and notes that open, relaxed postures and warmth are linked to impressions of trust.[1] Research on thin slices of behaviour, begun by Nalini Ambady and Robert Rosenthal in 1992, found that observers form reasonably accurate impressions of interpersonal traits from clips of a few seconds, which is the scientific backdrop for the idea that a person's bearing is read almost instantly.[3]

The idea reached a very wide audience through power posing: in a 2012 TED talk Amy Cuddy proposed that holding expansive poses makes people feel more powerful.[2][4] Later research found a reliable effect on how people feel but no reliable effect on hormones and an unclear effect on behaviour.[2][2] On looksmax.org, members write guides on 'charismamaxxing' that pair body language with voice tone and humour, and threads on reading interest and indifference in others.[5][6]

paras: Body language is the set of physical behaviours that accompany or replace speech. Wikipedia lists posture, gait, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch, breathing and the use of space among them, and notes that unlike sign languages it has no grammar and so is not a language in the linguistic sense.[1] Practitioners of presence training treat these behaviours as trainable habits: a slumped, hurried or closed bearing can be replaced with an upright, unhurried and open one.

In appearance terms the idea is that physical looks and bearing are perceived together. Someone who stands tall, moves calmly and meets others' eyes is described as seeming more attractive and more at ease than the same person hunched and fidgeting. The practice costs nothing and is typically done alongside posture work, grooming, fitness and clothing choices.

The formal study of body movement in communication is called kinesics. Anthropologist Ray Birdwhistell coined the term in 1952, filmed people in social situations, and proposed a unit of movement he called the kineme by analogy with the phoneme.[7] He estimated that words carry no more than 30 to 35 percent of a conversation's social meaning, concluded that kinesic displays have no universals, and disliked the popular term body language; Paul Ekman disputed the no-universals claim in his work on facial expressions.[7][1] Gestures, Birdwhistell held, are polysemic and cannot be decoded in any absolute way.[1]

Edward T. Hall introduced proxemics in 1966, dividing interpersonal distance into intimate, personal, social and public zones.[1] Hall's framework underlies advice about how close to stand and how much space to occupy.

Albert Mehrabian's 1967 studies are the source of the widely repeated 7%-38%-55% figures, which assign words, tone and facial expression shares of how much a speaker is liked when feelings are being communicated. Wikipedia notes that the figures combine two separate studies that used a single spoken word and photographs, involved only female participants and addressed only positive versus negative feelings, and that Mehrabian himself said the equations apply only to communication of feelings and attitudes.[8] The figures are nonetheless often cited as proof that most of a message is nonverbal.[8][6]

Reports note that leaning forward and nodding suggests openness, folded arms are often read as a closed mind, and relaxed hands suggest confidence.[1] Firm handshakes are said to improve the accuracy of first impressions.[1] Head tilt can be read as interest or suspicion, and posture and gait can reflect mood.[1]

Eye contact is often read as sincerity in workplaces, but meaning varies by culture, with prolonged gaze seen as a challenge or anger in some cultures.[1] The same gesture can differ in meaning: arms akimbo may signal relaxed confidence in Western countries but is considered rude in Bali.[1] A family-medicine review on cross-cultural care lists attitudes toward personal space, eye contact and body language among the areas where expectations differ between cultures.[9] Kinesics scholarship likewise notes that interpretations vary by culture, so misreading is a risk in intercultural settings.[7]

Ambady and Rosenthal's 1992 meta-analysis introduced the term thin slice for a brief sample of expressive behaviour. In 1993 they showed raters 2-, 5- and 10-second clips of teachers' nonverbal behaviour and found the ratings closely matched those of people with substantial contact, with clip length making no significant difference.[3] Wikipedia reports that thin-slicing works best for observable interpersonal traits such as dominance or shyness and less well for traits such as conscientiousness or intelligence, and that in this literature physical attractiveness mattered less when expressive behaviour was visible.[3]

Practitioners cite this literature to argue that bearing is evaluated quickly and that changing it changes the impression made. Malcolm Gladwell's book Blink popularised the idea of snap judgments to a general audience, though Wikipedia notes that some of its supporting claims have been criticised.[3]

In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap published a Psychological Science study of 42 participants reporting higher testosterone and lower cortisol after expansive poses, and suggested benefits for job interviews and negotiation.[2] Cuddy's 2012 TED talk reached a very large audience, with about 47 million views by 2017, and her 2015 book Presence reached number three on the New York Times advice best-seller list in February 2016.[2][4]

A 2015 replication by Eva Ranehill and colleagues found an effect on felt power but not on hormones, risk tolerance or behaviour.[2] In 2016 Carney stated that she no longer believed the effect was real, and Simonsohn and Simmons argued that it disappeared once selective reporting was accounted for.[2] Cuddy and colleagues published a 2018 analysis of 55 studies arguing for evidential value for effects on feelings and has continued to defend the research.[2][4] A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies by Körner and colleagues reported reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, no effect on physiological measures and an unclear behavioural effect, noting that few studies included a neutral-posture control.[2] Critics have also pointed out that many experiments compared expansive poses only with slouched ones, so they cannot show that expansive poses themselves help.[2]

A looksmax.org guide to charismamaxxing argues that charisma can make a difference to dating, jobs and friendships even for tall, conventionally attractive men, and splits it into body language, voice tonality and humour.[6] It cites the 7%-38%-55% split attributed to Mehrabian.[6][8]

Another thread, by a member who says he has studied body language for months, lists signs he associates with interest, such as preening, frequent eye contact and nervous behaviour, while noting that no single sign is conclusive.[5] Further threads cover mirroring and social-skills guides.[10][11] Outside the forum, a 2012 Hacker News discussion titled 'How Studying Body Language Changed the Way I Socialize' drew 188 points and 94 comments, showing the same self-improvement interest in general tech communities.[12]

Scholars disagree whether body language is universal, and Mehrabian's 7%-38%-55% split is widely debated.[1][8] Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that nonverbal cues reliably detect lies, though some law enforcement agencies still use them.[1] A 2021 BJPsych International review observed that people may be less skilled at reading others' faces and body language than they think.[13]
No studies found for presence training as a looks-related intervention. Related laboratory research on power posing and thin-slice judgments is summarised above.[2][3]

lore.intro: Body language is discussed on looksmax.org as part of 'charisma' and social skills, often alongside voice and humour, with members sharing guides on how to project confidence and read others.[5][6]
